citation.title: Procedural justice and (in)equitable participation in climate negotiations
citation.type: journal article (web version, with appendix table and two open peer reviews); published 2025-02-05

question: Whether small Party delegations are disadvantaged in UN climate negotiations from a procedural justice view: what delegation size is sufficient (about 15), how many Parties send fewer, and how to make the negotiations more equitable. It does not set out to measure business or fossil-fuel presence.
data: Official UNFCCC lists of participants for the eight COPs from COP21 (2015) to COP28 (2023); delegation size per Party per COP (Table A1 in the page, numeric, only its start was viewed). Income and population figures are used for the correlations; their sources are not named in the text read.
method: Descriptive analysis of delegation size (number of people listed under each Party): averages, frequencies, count of Parties at or below 15, Spearman rank correlations with income and population. The threshold of 15 comes from a normative argument and earlier literature (survey of AOSIS negotiators, a least-developed-country negotiator's view, UNFairplay report), and the authors call it a rough estimate. No classification of delegates by employer or sector.

definitions.definition: About 15 delegates, the number below which a delegation is very likely to struggle; the authors say it is a rough, somewhat arbitrary estimate.
definitions.quote: we chose 15 delegates as a threshold below which it becomes very likely that the respective delegation will struggle in the negotiations.
definitions.page: Procedural justice in the climate negotiations

definitions.definition: The number of people listed for a Party in the official lists of participants, used as a proxy for negotiation capacity, not as a count of negotiators.
definitions.quote: we maintain that delegation size is a widely used and useful proxy

proxies.indicator: Number of delegates listed under the Party in the official UNFCCC lists of participants.
proxies.quote: we use the official lists of participants, focusing on the last eight COPs since 2015.

findings.claim: Average delegation size rose from six to seven in 1995-1999 to 61 over 2015-2023.
findings.quote: Delegations comprised on average six to seven delegates in the first years of the negotiations (1995–1999).

findings.claim: Some Party delegations include private-sector representatives, including fossil fuel companies and other carbon-intensive industries. This is stated in one sentence, with two cited sources (Kick Big Polluters Out web pages on COP27 and COP28), and is not measured in the article.
findings.quote: Some government delegations also include representatives from the private sector, including fossil fuel companies and other carbon-intensive industries

findings.claim: Official lists include people who are not negotiators: security or logistics staff and civil society members accredited through the government.
findings.quote: not all delegates listed in the official lists of participants are technical negotiators.

findings.claim: 31 Parties had average delegations below 15 over COP21 to COP28.
findings.quote: Here, 31 parties have delegations that are on average below 15.

findings.claim: Mega-delegations are rising: delegations of 300 or more went from three at COP21 to ten at COP28.
findings.quote: while three countries had sent more than 300 delegates to COP21 in Paris (2015), the number of such delegations increased to 10 at the most recent COP.

limitations.point: Full article text and appendix table are present in the file, but the article contains no data or method on business or fossil-fuel presence; only the one sentence above and a peer reviewer's remark mention it. Nothing here answers Q1 or Q2 with numbers.
Delegation size is a crude measure and the lists mix negotiators with other people, including NGO members.
limitations.quote: Admittedly, delegation size is a crude measure of negotiation capacity.

limitations.point: The analysis is illustrative, not systematic.
limitations.quote: The above analysis serves mainly illustrative purposes; our aim here is not a comprehensive and systematic analysis of delegation size and its drivers.

limitations.point: A peer reviewer asked whether data on the composition of delegations exist; the article does not provide a composition breakdown.
limitations.quote: Do you have data on the compositions of delegations?
limitations.page: Open peer review from Kilian de Ridder

limitations.point: A peer reviewer suggested the paper note non-governmental delegates inside country delegations and the fossil fuel delegation. This is the reviewer's assertion, not a finding of the article, and the authors' response is not in the file.
limitations.quote: the presence of non-governmental delegates as part of country delegation.
limitations.page: Open peer review from Dan Osborn
